content: Heliox is a breathing gas composed of a mixture of helium (He) and oxygen (O2). It has been utilized in medical settings since the 1930s. Initially, its use was focused on alleviating symptoms of upper airway obstruction. However, over time, its applications in medicine have expanded significantly, primarily due to the gas's low density. Heliox is also employed in saturation diving and occasionally during the deep phases of technical dives. In medical practice, the term heliox typically refers to a mixture containing 21% oxygen (the same concentration as in ambient air) and 79% helium, although other mixtures are available. Airway resistance is influenced by both the diameter of the airways and the density of the gas being inhaled. When nitrogen, a component of air, is replaced with helium, the density of the inspired gas decreases, leading to a reduction in airway resistance. Consequently, breathing heliox reduces airway resistance and decreases the mechanical energy required to ventilate the lungs, also known as the Work of Breathing (WOB). Heliox is primarily used to manage medical conditions that involve a reduction in airway diameter, which increases airway resistance. These conditions include upper airway obstruction, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), bronchiolitis, and croup. Patients with these conditions may experience symptoms such as dyspnea (shortness of breath), hypoxemia (low oxygen levels in arterial blood), and respiratory muscle fatigue due to exhaustion. If untreated, these symptoms can progress to respiratory failure, necessitating intubation and mechanical ventilation. Heliox can mitigate these effects by making it easier for patients to breathe and reducing the Work of Breathing, thereby helping to prevent respiratory failure. Additionally, heliox has been found useful in weaning patients off mechanical ventilation and in enhancing the delivery of inhalable drugs through nebulization.
